notes.title: The Maker Way Open Playtest Starts Today
notes.content: [p]The first open playtest for The Maker Way starts today — come build, print, and pilot your own machines.[/p][p align="start"]After a successful closed playtest and great feedback from our amazing growing community, it’s time to put The Maker Way in more hands and shape what comes next.[/p][h2]Game Mechanics[/h2][p align="start"]Most core mechanics are already in. This playtest will let us see how they hold up before we expand them and add more content.[/p][p align="start"]What’s in now:[/p][list][*][p][i]Machine Design[/i] - Use a library of parts to build rovers, drones, and more.[/p][/*][*][p][i]Machine Operation[/i] - 3D-print the machines you designed and take them into an open world to complete tasks.[/p][/*][*][p][i]Resource & Energy[/i] [i]Management[/i] - Mine resources and produce energy to print more machines and keep them powered.[/p][/*][*][p][i]Base Building[/i] - Build bases to store resources, extend remote-control range with antennas, and run research on servers.[/p][/*][*][p][i]Part Discovery & Research[/i] - Research to add parts to your tech tree, and scan parts in the open world to unlock new specs.[/p][/*][/list][h2]Other Mechanics[/h2][list][*][p][i]Remote-Control Range[/i] — Stay close or extend coverage by building base antennas.[/p][/*][*][p][i]Combat[/i] — Use weapon parts to fight the three enemies currently on the scene guarding the government base.[/p][/*][/list]

notes.title: Maker Log #2 - Why I waited with external playtests for 18 more months
notes.content:
I’ve been working on The Maker Way for more than four years now. Given that I started with zero knowledge in game dev, the first couple of years were really focused on getting to learn Unity, Blender, C#, Animation, Environment Design etc… you get the point.

At some point I really need to pen down a blog post about the history of the game. There are some really amusing videos from very early builds :)

In June last year, I posted an early alpha version to Itch.IO. Some people played it and gave me good feedback, but I realized something important - they were not playing the game that I wanted to make, they were playing the game that I was capable of producing at that point.

I really value care and excellence being put into products and I just hated that I put out something that I wasn’t proud of because I felt pressure to get some playtesters.

So I took the time and went back to the lab, or to be accurate more of a small home office.

Been building and testing and building more and testing more for the last 18 months. This goes against every advice from some incredible game developers such as Jonas Tyroller (really recommend his Youtube channel if you are into gamedev) and others. But I took comfort in knowing that at least one game dev took a similar approach - Eric Barone, who made Stardew Valley:

[i]Traditionally, video games are playtested extensively—dozens, if not hundreds, of people kicking the tires, looking for bugs and issues. But even more than that, games are a form of art built on complex systems and code. Playtesters are often asked, Is this game even fun to play?
Remarkably, Eric was the only person to play Stardew Valley until the very last stages.[/i]
[b] - Eric Barone - GQ Profile[/b]

And several days ago, 18 months later, I finally got a decent playtest version up and running on Steam. I also started giving out keys to play testers.

I’m still very far from the vision and aspiration I have for the game but it is a good point to iterate from.

From here, the plan is to have regular updates while gradually expanding the approved playtesters pool until the game is ready for a full on demo, and later, Early Access.

notes.title: New playtest version available! You can even win a t-shirt!
notes.content:
The day is here - looking for new signtups to our first community playtest!

While I did ran several small playtesting sesssions, this is going to be the first playtest that is open to the community.

I still intend to have only a couple dozen playtests this round but expect to grow the list over the next several months.

Please head over to the [url=https://themakerway.com/playtest/]playtest page[/url] to sign up and I’ll follow up personally.

This version has massive changes compared to the last version:

[olist]
[*] Overhauled environment with deeper simulation - improved global illumination, vegetation, ambient sounds
[*] Improved machine design editor - easier to use machine editor with shortcuts and new additional parts
[*] Introduction of a player character (the last playtest version was machines only!) - probably the biggest change since the last version. It makes the game so much more dynamic because the player can interact with the machines they build
[*] Resource collection and management - this was planned for quite a while but the game includes 6 key resources for you to collect. You need them to build new machines
[*] Basic base building - allowing you to build chargers and fuel stations for your machines across the map
[*] Looking forward to hearing your thoughts!
[/olist]

notes.title: Devlog #0 - Why make this game?
notes.content:
On October 9th, 1903, the New York Times published an article predicting that it would take between [b]1 million to 10 million years[/b] to achieve human flight. 

[b]Exactly 2 months and 8 days later[/b], on December 17, 1903, the Wright Brothers flew for the first time.

As a father, I'd like for my kids to grow in world where we believe in our ability to invent, create and make a better future for ourselves. I started thinking what type of game could excite players about making and inventing. After a couple of weeks of sitting down with only pen and paper, trying to figure out the concept, it dawned on me:  a sandbox game about building and crafting, where players can build creative machines and robots in response to missions.

But the game's setting was also important. Originally the setting was in space, and the missions a bit mundane. Then, I realized that the best setting for the game is right here on Earth. It's about facing real challenges and using your problem-solving skills and hard work to make this world a better place.

It's always day 1 on this journey and we're excited about the work on the game moving forward, and within a couple of months, getting the community's feedback on our alpha version.
